marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q013.takeaway: Erythropoietic protoporphyria accumulates heme intermediates in erythroid cells, not primarily in liver.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q013.displayText: Porphyrias are grouped by where excess heme-pathway intermediates accumulate. In erythropoietic porphyrias, overproduction occurs mainly in bone-marrow erythroid cells; these often present early with cutaneous photosensitivity. Examples include congenital erythropoietic porphyria, erythropoietic protoporphyria and X-linked protoporphyria. Hepatic porphyrias accumulate intermediates mainly in liver. Acute hepatic forms, including acute intermittent, hereditary coproporphyria, variegate and ALA-dehydratase-deficiency porphyrias, can cause neurovisceral attacks; chronic porphyria cutanea tarda commonly causes adult-onset blistering photosensitivity.

rationales.a: Variegate porphyria is hepatic and can cause acute neurovisceral episodes as well as photosensitivity.
rationales.b: Acute intermittent porphyria is an acute hepatic porphyria with neurovisceral attacks from hepatic ALA and porphobilinogen accumulation.
rationales.c: Porphyria cutanea tarda is a chronic hepatic porphyria with adult-onset blistering photosensitivity.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q014.takeaway: Infantile photosensitivity with erythrodontia points to congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther disease).
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q014.displayText: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther disease) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency. Porphyrin I isomers accumulate in erythrocytes, marrow, plasma, urine and teeth, causing severe photosensitivity and red-brown teeth (erythrodontia) that fluoresce under ultraviolet light. Infants may have port-wine urine or pink-stained diapers; severe fetal disease can cause nonimmune hydrops. Delayed tooth eruption and early blistering photosensitivity in this vignette support the diagnosis.

rationales.b: Porphyria cutanea tarda is a hepatic UROD-deficiency disorder that usually presents in adults with blistering photosensitivity, not congenital erythrodontia.
rationales.c: Erythropoietic protoporphyria generally causes nonblistering photosensitivity and protoporphyrin accumulation; it does not cause the characteristic porphyrin-stained teeth.
rationales.d: Acute intermittent porphyria causes neurovisceral attacks from hepatic precursor accumulation and does not produce early cutaneous photosensitivity or erythrodontia.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q015.takeaway: Gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations cause X-linked protoporphyria; loss-of-function ALAS2 causes sideroblastic anemia.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q015.displayText: X-linked protoporphyria is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in ALA synthase 2 (ALAS2), leading to increased enzyme activity and ALA synthesis. When iron incorporation becomes limiting, protoporphyrin is not converted to heme and accumulates. ALAS2 mutations are also seen in X-linked sideroblastic anemia, which is not a porphyria: a loss-of-function mutation decreases ALAS2 activity and protoporphyrin synthesis. Sphingolipids are amphipathic and are found in the outer plasma-membrane leaflet and myelin sheath; they also participate in cell signaling and apoptosis.

rationales.a: Acute intermittent porphyria is due to HMBS deficiency and is typically autosomal dominant, not caused by an ALAS2 variant.
rationales.b: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria is due to uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency and is autosomal recessive.
rationales.d: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is commonly associated with deficient ferrochelatase activity; the X-linked protoporphyria option specifically reflects ALAS2 gain of function.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q016.takeaway: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes variegate porphyria, an autosomal-dominant acute hepatic porphyria.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q016.displayText: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase is defective in variegate porphyria. Variegate porphyria is an autosomal dominant porphyria. Protoporphyrinogen IX accumulates in the urine. Patients present with acute attacks of abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy; cutaneous photosensitivity is also seen.

rationales.a: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes hereditary coproporphyria, another acute hepatic porphyria, but it is a different enzyme block.
rationales.c: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther disease), not variegate porphyria.
rationales.d: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, which usually presents with chronic blistering photosensitivity.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q017.takeaway: Heme oxygenase opens the porphyrin ring, producing biliverdin while releasing carbon monoxide and ferrous iron.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q017.displayText: Heme oxygenase initiates heme catabolism in the endoplasmic-reticulum system of reticuloendothelial cells. Oxidative cleavage of the porphyrin ring forms biliverdin and releases carbon monoxide and iron. Biliverdin reductase then uses NADPH to convert biliverdin to bilirubin; iron is conserved and stored or recycled. Heme oxygenase is the principal enzymatic source of endogenous carbon monoxide.

rationales.a: Biliverdin reductase converts biliverdin to bilirubin using NADPH; this reduction does not cleave heme or release carbon monoxide.
rationales.c: Bilirubin conjugation with glucuronic acid occurs in hepatocytes and does not release carbon monoxide.
rationales.d: A second glucuronyl transfer forms bilirubin diglucuronide from the monoglucuronide; carbon monoxide is produced upstream during heme-ring cleavage.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q018.takeaway: Hepatic UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid in the endoplasmic reticulum.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q018.displayText: The endoplasmic reticulum is the site for bilirubin conjugation. Hepatocytes convert bilirubin to a polar form by conjugation. UDP-glucuronic acid acts as the glucuronyl donor, first producing bilirubin monoglucuronide and then bilirubin diglucuronide, which is excreted in bile. The reaction is catalyzed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) in the ER.

rationales.a: Cytosol is involved in bilirubin uptake and transport, but the conjugating enzyme UGT1A1 is located in the ER.
rationales.c: Mitochondria carry out the initial and final heme-synthesis steps; they are not the site of hepatic bilirubin glucuronidation.
rationales.d: The Golgi modifies and sorts many secretory products, but bilirubin conjugation occurs earlier in the hepatocyte ER.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q019.takeaway: Canalicular MRP2-mediated secretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile is the rate-limiting hepatic step in the source account.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q019.displayText: After UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin in the endoplasmic reticulum, hepatocytes actively export bilirubin glucuronides across the canalicular membrane into bile. Multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP2/ABCC2) mediates this ATP-dependent transport. The source identifies canalicular secretion as the rate-limiting step in hepatic bilirubin metabolism. Failure of this transporter causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, as in Dubin–Johnson syndrome.

rationales.a: Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin in plasma to the liver; this transport is upstream and is not the source-keyed rate-limiting hepatic step.
rationales.b: Hepatic uptake transfers albumin-released bilirubin into hepatocytes, but the source identifies canalicular export of the conjugate as rate-limiting.
rationales.c: UGT1A1 conjugation makes bilirubin water-soluble in the ER; it precedes the source-keyed active secretion into bile.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q020.takeaway: The Van den Bergh diazo reaction measures bilirubin and distinguishes conjugated from unconjugated fractions.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q020.displayText: The Van den Bergh reaction is a diazo colorimetric method for serum bilirubin. Diazotized sulfanilic acid reacts with bilirubin to form colored azodipyrroles. Conjugated bilirubin reacts directly in aqueous reagent; unconjugated bilirubin reacts after an accelerator such as methanol is added. Ehrlich's test detects urobilinogen, Hay's test detects urinary bile salts, and Benedict's test detects reducing sugars.

rationales.a: Ehrlich's aldehyde reagent is used to detect urobilinogen in urine or feces, not to measure serum bilirubin.
rationales.c: Hay's sulfur test detects bile salts in urine; it is not the serum bilirubin diazo assay.
rationales.d: Benedict's reagent detects reducing substances such as glucose; it is not a bilirubin measurement test.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q021.takeaway: Pancreatic-head obstruction causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, giving a direct-positive Van den Bergh reaction.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q021.displayText: A palpable upper-abdominal mass with jaundice, pruritus and scratch marks suggests extrahepatic biliary obstruction, including pancreatic-head malignancy. Obstruction prevents conjugated bilirubin from reaching the intestine and causes it to reflux into blood. Because conjugated bilirubin reacts with diazo reagent without an accelerator such as methanol, the Van den Bergh reaction is direct positive. Pale stools and dark urine may accompany obstructive cholestasis.

rationales.b: An indirect-positive reaction indicates predominantly unconjugated bilirubin, as in hemolysis or impaired conjugation, rather than obstructive cholestasis.
rationales.c: A biphasic reaction can occur when conjugated and unconjugated fractions are both elevated, but the obstructive pattern here is direct-predominant.
rationales.d: The marked jaundice and likely biliary obstruction produce circulating conjugated bilirubin, so the diazo test is expected to react rather than remain negative.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q022.takeaway: Dubin–Johnson syndrome is caused by impaired canalicular export of conjugated bilirubin from MRP2 deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q022.displayText: Dubin–Johnson syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss of canalicular multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP2/ABCC2). Impaired export of conjugated bilirubin produces predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a coarse, darkly pigmented liver. This is the source's diagnostic clue. The stem mentions laboratory values that are not present in the canonical question record; no missing value or pattern is inferred.

rationales.a: OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 mediate hepatic uptake of bilirubin and other organic anions; their deficiency causes Rotor syndrome rather than a black liver.
rationales.b: BSEP (ABCB11) exports bile salts; its deficiency causes familial cholestasis, not the conjugated bilirubin transport defect of Dubin–Johnson syndrome.
rationales.c: MRP3 is a basolateral transporter that can export conjugates back toward blood; the canalicular exporter deficient in Dubin–Johnson syndrome is MRP2.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q023.takeaway: Stress-triggered mild unconjugated jaundice in a healthy young adult is typical of Gilbert syndrome from reduced UGT1A1 expression.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q023.displayText: A healthy young adult with transient jaundice after a viral febrile illness and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia most likely has Gilbert syndrome. The common mechanism is a promoter defect in the UGT1A1 gene, reducing transcription of the normal enzyme; residual activity is about 10–33% of normal. Mild unconjugated bilirubin elevation may recur with stress, alcohol or reduced caloric intake while other liver tests remain normal. The source also notes increased hepatic lipofuscin, a response to phenobarbital, and that treatment is not usually required; bilirubin can fluctuate and jaundice generally resolves without ill effects.
emphasis: promoter defect in the UGT1A1 gene

rationales.a: BSEP deficiency impairs bile-salt export and causes cholestatic disease, not isolated stress-triggered unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
rationales.b: MRP2 deficiency causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in Dubin–Johnson syndrome, opposite to the bilirubin fraction in this vignette.
rationales.d: A severe missense defect with minimal UGT1A1 activity is more characteristic of Crigler–Najjar syndrome; Gilbert syndrome most often reflects reduced promoter-driven expression.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q024.takeaway: Complete biliary obstruction prevents urobilinogen formation, so urine urobilinogen is absent or markedly reduced.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH17_Q024.displayText: In complete extrahepatic obstruction, conjugated bilirubin cannot enter the gut, so intestinal bacteria cannot convert it to urobilinogen. Urinary urobilinogen is therefore absent or markedly reduced, while water-soluble conjugated bilirubin refluxes into plasma and appears in urine. Hemolysis instead increases bilirubin delivery to the liver but produces unconjugated bilirubin, which is not filtered into urine. Hepatocellular disease can produce variable urinary urobilinogen depending on uptake, excretion and intrahepatic cholestasis.

rationales.a: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and water-insoluble, so it does not appear in urine during hemolytic jaundice; this statement is true.
rationales.c: Crigler–Najjar syndrome reflects deficient UGT1A1 activity and causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; this statement is true.
rationales.d: Hepatocellular disease may yield normal or reduced urinary urobilinogen when hepatocyte injury or intrahepatic cholestasis limits bile flow; this can be true.
